items.why: Directly contrasts the Levite’s stated purpose with the place he later happens to reach.
The blessing is identifiable, but calling it a “request” and locating it just before the fire call is awkward.
Clearly tests who uttered the curse despite Micah being the current speaker.
Micah explicitly gives the Levite’s becoming his priest as the reason for his expectation.
Clearly distinguishes the relatives receiving the instruction from the citizens receiving the message.
Strongly separates the reported news that prompted the ambush from what Abimelek observed afterward.
The secret sender and the rival named in his message are explicit and easily confused roles.
Tests Abimelek’s specific purpose in approaching the entrance rather than his broader attack.
“Does something” is too vague to identify a meaningful action or comprehension target.
The olive tree explicitly links its refusal to giving up its honoring oil.
The correction is clear, though the question’s pronoun is awkward and the key says hills rather than mountains.
Effectively distinguishes whom the mother says will make the image from the silversmith who actually makes it.
The fatal cause is explicit and distinct from the occupants’ earlier movement into the stronghold.
The fig tree’s reason is explicit, though this closely duplicates the neighboring olive-tree refusal pattern.
Clearly distinguishes the duration of the priesthood from the separately stated duration of idol use.
The curse appears as the means or culmination of punishment, not clearly as something occurring afterward.
Jotham’s fear of Abimelek is stated directly as the reason he lives in Beer.
The sequence supports the answer, but the question is cumbersome and asks for a broad region as a preceding place.
The servant’s action clearly kills Abimelek, though the distinction is fairly elementary.
Strong sequence test distinguishing the five men’s initial taking from the priest’s later handling of the objects.
The shouting is the immediate trigger for turning, distinct from the earlier overtaking.
The referent is recoverable as Jerub-Baal, though “the man” is not the passage’s own wording.
The passage directly attributes prosperity to the land lacking nothing, not to Sidonian-style living.
The lack of rescue is explicitly explained by distance from Sidon and absence of outside ties.
The priest is identifiable from his reply, but the opening pronoun lacks an explicit antecedent in the window.
Precisely distinguishes the five spies who enter and take the objects from those remaining at the gate.
Jotham explicitly states that their listening should result in God listening to them.
The object of “take it over” is clearly the land rather than its unsuspecting inhabitants.
The causal statement clearly distinguishes lack of inheritance from the incidental absence of a king.
The requested kingship over the trees is clear, but the competitor is implausible and offers little discrimination.
Strongly distinguishes the festival activity during the cursing from the earlier grape work.
